title: How to Warm Up Email Accounts for Cold Outreach
metaTitle: How to Warm Up Email Accounts (2026)
metaDescription: What email warmup actually does, the ramp schedule that works, how long the process really takes, and the mistakes that waste it. A hands-on guide to warming up cold email accounts.
excerpt: Warmup is how you convince mailbox providers you're a real sender before you start running real campaigns. Skip it and even a flawlessly configured account still lands in spam. Here's how to do it properly.

toc.title: Why new accounts can't skip it
Doing it manually vs automating it
When warmup alone won't cut it

contentHtml:
Warmup is the process of earning a sending reputation for a new email account before you ever put it to work on real campaigns. It works by sending a small, slowly growing volume of mail that actually gets opened and replied to, which teaches mailbox providers that a legitimate sender is behind the account.

It's also the step people are most tempted to cut corners on, mainly because it's slow and produces nothing you can point to right away. Skipping it happens to also be the fastest way to send a flawlessly configured account straight into spam.

What warmup actually does

A mailbox provider decides how much to trust a sender based on history. A brand-new account has no history at all, which means it has no trust either. Warmup is how you manufacture that history in a controlled, deliberate way.

In practice, this means the account trades real emails back and forth with other genuine accounts. Those messages get opened, replied to, and pulled out of spam if they happen to land there. Every one of those interactions is a positive signal, and reputation is really just the steady buildup of them over time.

Why new accounts can't skip it

Acting like an established sender is itself something you have to earn, not something you can claim on day one. If a mailbox that's one day old suddenly fires off 500 emails, that pattern looks nothing like a real human being and everything like a spammer standing up a burner account.

This applies just as much to new domains as it does to new mailboxes on an existing domain, and to accounts coming back from a deliverability problem. Any account without a recent, healthy sending history needs to go through warmup before it's allowed to carry real campaign volume.

The ramp schedule that works

Warmup follows a gradual ramp, not some fixed target number. The exact figures shift depending on provider and account age, but the overall shape stays consistent: start very low, climb slowly, and never jump.

  • Week 1. Just a handful of warmup emails per mailbox each day. The goal here is showing the first signs of activity, not chasing volume.
  • Week 2. Ramp up steadily, staying well under campaign-level volume. Keep an eye on whether the mail is actually landing in the inbox rather than spam.
  • Week 3. Keep the ramp going and start layering in a small amount of real campaign volume alongside the ongoing warmup.
  • Ongoing. Keep warmup running underneath your campaigns permanently. It's a maintenance signal, not just something you do once during onboarding.

You can model out target volume for your specific mailbox count using the free warmup calculator.

How long it really takes

Budget two to three weeks before a new account is ready to carry meaningful campaign volume. There's no way around this timeline. Anyone claiming they can hand you a fully warmed account in three days is selling you a number, not an actual reputation.

The account isn't finished at the end of week three, either. Warmup keeps running at a lighter level underneath your real sending going forward, because an abrupt stop in warmup activity is itself a noticeable change in pattern.

It varies by provider

One ramp schedule doesn't fit every mailbox equally well. Google, Outlook, and Azure mailboxes each respond differently, so the volume you ramp toward and the reply rate you're targeting need to be tuned per provider instead of applied uniformly.

Microsoft mailboxes — both Outlook and Microsoft 365 — tend to be noticeably more sensitive than Gmail. They handle a slower ramp and a lower steady-state volume better, and pushing them at Gmail's pace is a common way to stall a Microsoft mailbox out. Gmail and Google Workspace mailboxes generally tolerate a somewhat faster ramp once the early signals look healthy. Azure-hosted mailboxes are their own case again, with different tolerances entirely. Treating all three identically will end up over-pushing some mailboxes while under-warming others.

This is one more reason to lean on automated warmup that's actually provider-aware. Sendbox's human-like warmup adjusts both ramp volume and reply rate per provider, so a Microsoft mailbox is never forced onto a Gmail-paced schedule.

Doing it manually vs automating it

You can warm up an account manually by emailing colleagues and contacts on a set schedule, but that approach falls apart past a couple of mailboxes and is easy to run inconsistently. Automated warmup handles the ramp for you across every mailbox at once.

The gap between warmup tools is real and worth paying attention to. Older tools just fire off a fixed schedule regardless of what's actually happening with the account. Sendbox's human-like warmup varies timing and volume so it looks organic, and it throttles automatically when account health dips, so warmup actively heals the mailbox instead of pushing it harder while it's already struggling.

Mistakes that waste your warmup

  • Skipping it entirely. The big one. A perfectly clean setup with no warmup still ends up in spam.
  • Ramping too aggressively. Jumping straight from warmup into full campaign volume undoes all the work you just put in. That transition needs to be gradual too.
  • Cutting warmup off once campaigns start. Warmup is ongoing maintenance, not a task you check off during onboarding and forget.
  • Running warmup while ignoring what the data says. If a mailbox is landing warmup mail in spam, that's telling you to slow down, not push through it.
  • Warming up a fundamentally broken setup. Warmup can't compensate for missing authentication or the wrong domain. Fix the foundation first.

When warmup alone won't cut it

Warmup builds reputation, but it can't rescue a broken foundation underneath it. If your authentication is missing, your domain choice is wrong, or you're sending to a list you never validated, warmup won't save you from any of that.

It also can't fully insulate you on a shared IP pool, where other senders are influencing the same reputation you're trying to build up. Warmup is one layer in a much larger system — pair it with solid infrastructure and authentication, and get the full picture from the deliverability guide and the infrastructure setup guide.

faqs.question: How long does it take to warm up a new email account?
faqs.answer: Budget two to three weeks before a new account is ready for real campaign volume. Warmup is a gradual ramp, starting from a handful of emails per day and working up toward campaign-level volume, and it genuinely can't be rushed safely.

faqs.question: Do I need to keep warmup running after I start sending campaigns?
faqs.answer: Yes. Warmup is ongoing maintenance, not a one-time onboarding step. Keep it running at a lighter level underneath your real campaigns, since an abrupt stop in warmup activity is itself a noticeable shift in your sending pattern.

faqs.question: Can I warm up an email account manually?
faqs.answer: You can, by emailing real contacts on a consistent schedule, but it stops scaling past one or two mailboxes and is easy to do unevenly. Automated warmup runs the ramp reliably across every mailbox at the same time.

faqs.question: Does warmup fix bad deliverability?
faqs.answer: Only the piece caused by a missing reputation. Warmup can't repair broken authentication, the wrong sending domain, or a list you never validated. Fix the foundation first — warmup then builds the reputation on top of that.

faqs.question: How many warmup emails per day should I send?
faqs.answer: Start with just a handful per mailbox in week one, then increase steadily from there. The exact figure depends on the provider and the account's age. The underlying principle is: start low, and never jump volume sharply.

faqs.question: Does warmup work the same for Gmail, Outlook, and Azure mailboxes?
faqs.answer: No. Microsoft mailboxes, including Outlook and Microsoft 365, are generally more sensitive than Gmail and need a slower, lower-volume ramp. Azure-hosted mailboxes are different again. Ramp volume and reply rates for warmup should be tuned per provider, not applied the same way across every mailbox.

faqs.question: Is it safe to warm up and send campaigns from the same mailbox?
faqs.answer: Yes, once the mailbox is past its initial ramp. By week three you can start layering a small amount of campaign volume alongside ongoing warmup, then increase campaign volume gradually while warmup keeps running in the background.
